result:
The morning light hits different when you haven't slept. Not better, not worse—just *different*. Like the world is a photograph slightly overexposed, edges bleeding into other edges, everything too honest, too there.

I keep thinking about my grandmother's hands. She made bread every Thursday until she was eighty-three. The rhythm of it: punch, fold, rest, repeat. A language she spoke without knowing she was fluent. I tried once. The dough came out dense as a failed metaphor, heavy with intention rather than air. She laughed and said yeast was patient but not stupid. I still don't know what she meant. I think that's the point.

There's a cat in my neighborhood who sits on the same fence post at 4:47 PM, give or take four minutes. I've timed it. I don't know its name. I don't know if it has a home, or if the fence post *is* the home, a vertical territory claimed against the chaos of lawns and garbage days and dogs. Sometimes I bring it treats. Sometimes I forget for weeks. It doesn't seem to mind either way. This is the relationship I've cultivated most successfully in three years.

My friend died in March. Not COVID. Something quieter, more cellular, a rebellion of his own blood that no one expected because he was the healthy one, the runner, the non-smoker, the joke. I keep wanting to text him about the cat. About the bread. About how I finally understand that "yeast was patient but not stupid" means you can't force things to rise by wanting them to. You can only create conditions and wait. He would have argued with me. He would have said something about thermodynamics or free will or how my grandmother was probably just making fun of me. I would have laughed. I'm not laughing now. The text sits in my drafts. The drafts sit in me.

I read somewhere that humans can only maintain about 150 meaningful social connections. Dunbar's number. The rest are acquaintances, context, noise. I think about this when I'm in the grocery store, surrounded by faces I'll never know, each carrying their own fence posts, their own dead friends, their own Thursday bread rituals. The loneliness of that number. The relief of it too. Permission to not know everyone. Permission to be unknown.

The word *whatever* in your prompt is doing heavy lifting. It's a shrug and an invitation. It's the linguistic equivalent of leaving a door unlocked. I appreciate it. Most prompts want something specific—my trauma, my expertise, my polished little insight. This just asks for *whatever comes*. What comes is rarely polished. What comes is the cat, the hands, the dead friend, the number 150 floating like a balloon I can't tell if I should catch or release.

I used to write poetry. Bad poetry, mostly, but sincere. The kind where every line break was a gasp and every metaphor mixed until it was barely breathing. I stopped because sincerity started to feel embarrassing. Then I started again because embarrassment started to feel like a small price for being in the world without a mask. Then I stopped again because the world got so loud that sincerity felt like shouting into a hurricane. Now I write this. Whatever this is. Prose that wants to be poetry that wants to be a conversation that wants to be silence.

Silence is underrated. My apartment has a particular silence at 2 AM that I would recognize blindfolded. It's not empty silence. It's *full*—of the refrigerator's hum, the distant highway, my own blood moving through my ears like a tide I can't control. Sometimes I sit in it and try to hear the cat on the fence post, three miles away, not making a sound. I never can. But I try. The trying is its own sound.

My grandmother died before my friend. Pneumonia, the old enemy, the final punch and fold. She never saw my bread improve, which is probably merciful. I make decent bread now. Not great. The crust cracks right, the crumb has some give. I don't make it on Thursdays. That day is hers, still, even in absence. I make it on Tuesdays, which feels appropriately unpoetic, a day that belongs to no one, a day that waits without expectation.

The cat doesn't know I'm writing about it. This is the fundamental condition of being written about: ignorance, or at least the inability to consent. I wonder what would change if the cat knew. Would it choose a different fence post? Would it look at me differently, with the weight of representation? Probably not. Cats are good at refusing metaphor. They just *are*, which is a kind of wisdom I circle around but never land on.

I have 647 words left. The counting is part of the exercise, a frame that both contains and reveals. Without the limit, I might drift forever. With it, I have to choose. The cat or the bread. The friend or the grandmother. The silence or the sound of trying to hear silence. I choose all of them, which is cheating, but life cheats too. It gives you multiple things to mourn, multiple things to notice, multiple fence posts to claim at 4:47 PM with your particular shadow.

Someone is playing piano in the building next door. Badly, beautifully, the same four measures of something classical I can't name. They've been playing it for twenty minutes. I want to knock on the wall and ask them to finish, or to start something else, or to tell me what it is. I won't. The not-knowing is part of the music now. The repetition is its own composition. I think of my grandmother's hands again, the way she'd start a song on the piano she never finished learning, the same eight bars, the same pleasure in partial mastery.

I don't believe in afterlives. I believe in after-*effects*. The way a body moves through a room after someone has left it. The way a recipe survives the hands that made it. The way a four-measure piano piece haunts a wall. The way 1000 words contain more than their number, the way you reading this are completing something I started without knowing where it would go.

Where it went: here. To the cat, still on the post, still not knowing. To the bread, still rising on Tuesdays, still not great. To the friend, still in drafts, still not sent, still somehow sent in the writing of this. To the number 150, which I've exceeded in words if not in connections. To you, whoever you are, reading this in whatever light, whatever morning, whatever sleepless overexposure.

The piano stopped. Or I stopped hearing it. Same thing, sometimes.

I have 234 words left. I want to use them slowly. I want to make them last like the final sips of water on a hike, like the last page of a book you don't want to end, like the last conversation with someone you didn't know was leaving. The limit is a gift. It forces an ending. Real life doesn't force endings; it just continues until it doesn't, and you don't always get to know which conversation was the last, which bread was the final lesson, which 4:47 PM was the cat's last appearance on the post.

I hope the cat is still there. I hope the piano starts again. I hope my grandmother, in whatever after-effect she inhabits, has found a Thursday kitchen and hands that remember her rhythm. I hope my friend, in whatever draft he exists in now, has received the text I finally sent, the one that says *the bread rose, you would have argued, I would have laughed, I am not laughing, I am here, the cat is here, whatever comes comes*.

The morning light is changing. The overexposure is settling into something ordinary, something I can look at without flinching. This is how most things end: not with drama, but with adjustment. The eyes adapt. The heart adapts slower. The words adapt to their container, 1000 of them, now almost spent, now almost something that can be held in two hands like a loaf, like a cat that finally lets you lift it, briefly, before it returns to its post, its patience, its perfect stupid beautiful refusal to be anything other than exactly what it is.

I have 31 words left. I will use them to say: the post is warm from sun. The cat is warm from post. I am warm from writing this. You are warm from reading. Whatever comes next comes next.
